# Introduction {#intro}

```{r species-image, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap="*Eriogonum longifolium var. gnaphalifolium. Image from Wikipedia.*"}

wiki_page <- "Eriogonum longifolium var. gnaphalifolium"

wiki_api <- paste0(
  "https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?",
  "action=query&format=json&prop=pageimages&",
  "piprop=thumbnail&pithumbsize=1400&titles=",
  URLencode(wiki_page, reserved = TRUE))

wiki_data <- jsonlite::fromJSON(
  wiki_api,
  simplifyVector = FALSE)

img_url <- wiki_data$query$pages[[1]]$thumbnail$source

dir.create("images", showWarnings = FALSE)

img_ext <- tools::file_ext(
  sub("\\?.*$", "", img_url))

img_file <- file.path(
  "images",
  paste0("eriogonum_wikipedia.", img_ext))

download.file(
  img_url,
  destfile = img_file,
  mode = "wb",
  quiet = TRUE)

knitr::include_graphics(img_file)
```

The supplementary material to the *Eriogonum longifolium* demographic dataset
from Archbold Biological Station.

The GIS and Data Management program at
[Archbold Biological Station](https://www.archbold-station.org/gis-and-data-mgmt/)
maintains a comprehensive collection of ecological and environmental data
gathered through research initiatives and long-term monitoring projects. One
key platform for accessing these data is the
[Environmental Data Initiative (EDI)](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/home.jsp),
which hosts long-term ecological datasets from Archbold Biological Station.

For our model, we utilized 24 years (1990--2013) of demographic data on scrub
buckwheat, [*Eriogonum longifolium* var. *gnaphalifolium*](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/mapbrowse?packageid=edi.226.1),
a threatened perennial herb endemic to periodically burned xeric uplands in
central peninsular Florida. The long-term dataset includes observations of
individual survival, growth, flowering, dormancy, recruitment, and responses to
prescribed fire, allowing us to incorporate both continuous plant size and
fire history into an integral projection model (IPM). :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

These demographic data have previously been used by Satterthwaite, Menges, and
Quintana-Ascencio (2002) in *Assessing scrub buckwheat population viability in
relation to fire using multiple modeling techniques*. Their study used
stage-structured matrix models and population viability analyses to evaluate
the effects of fire and fire-return intervals on the population dynamics of
*E. longifolium* var. *gnaphalifolium*. In the present analysis, we revisit the
long-term demographic record using an IPM framework to describe individual
demographic rates and their relationship with fire history.

# Data {#data}

## Dataset overview

The [dataset](https://portal.edirepository.org/nis/metadataviewer?packageid=edi.226.1)
documents long-term demographic monitoring of scrub buckwheat,
*Eriogonum longifolium* var. *gnaphalifolium*, in central peninsular Florida.
The working dataset spans 1990--2013 and contains repeated demographic
observations of individually marked plants together with observations from
prescribed fires.

*Eriogonum longifolium* var. *gnaphalifolium* is a perennial herb of xeric
uplands, including sandhill and Florida scrub. Plants consist of a basal rosette
and may produce one or several flowering scapes. Individuals possess a woody
taproot and can remain dormant belowground for one or more years before
reappearing aboveground. Fire is an important component of the species'
environment and can strongly affect its demographic rates, including growth and
flowering.

Individual plants were repeatedly monitored for survival and status, life-history
stage, basal rosette diameter, and flowering. Plants that were not visible were
not immediately removed from monitoring, allowing later reappearances to be
identified as periods of dormancy. New plants were also searched for and marked
during demographic censuses.

For the present analysis, the June-coded demographic census is used to construct
annual demographic transitions. Additional demographic observations, including
the September 1998 and December 2001 censuses, are retained where they provide
information on recruitment and fire responses. Fire observations occur as
separate event-specific records and include information on whether marked plant
locations were burned and, for later fires, whether plants were scorched or
consumed.

The earlier portion of these demographic data was analyzed by
[Satterthwaite et al. (2002)](https://doi.org/10.1890/1051-0761(2002)012%5B1672:ASBPVI%5D2.0.CO;2),
who used stage-structured matrix models to investigate the effects of fire on
population growth and viability. Their life-cycle representation included new,
small, vegetative, flowering, and dormant plants and explicitly distinguished
burned, year-after-burn, and unburned demographic transitions.

The data preparation below reconstructs annual demographic histories and derives
the variables required for the integral projection model, including survival,
growth, flowering, dormancy and reactivation, recruitment, and current and
previous fire exposure. Recruitment is reconstructed at the quadrat by
fecundity-year level and is combined with individual demographic observations in
the final working dataset using separate row types. This allows all information
required by the IPM to be retained in a single working-data object without
duplicating quadrat-level recruitment observations across individual plants.



## Data import and raw structure
The raw dataset contains 37,248 records. Of these, 34,146 are demographic
observations and 3,102 are observations associated with prescribed-fire events.
Demographic and fire observations are stored as separate records in the original
data and are therefore separated at the beginning of the data preparation.

Demographic observations span 1990--2013. The main annual census is recorded
in June, although additional demographic observations occur in September 1998
and December 2001. These additional censuses are retained because they contain
useful information on recruitment and post-fire demographic status, but the June
censuses form the basis of the annual demographic transitions used in the IPM.

Plant numbers are not globally unique across the dataset. We therefore define an
individual by the combination of site, population, quadrat, and plant number.
This results in 2,060 unique individual histories.

```{r}
df_og <- read_csv(
  file.path(dir_data, 'eriogonum_longifolium_data.csv'),
  col_types = cols(comment = col_character())) %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

# Keep the metadata table open until the EDI code definitions are confirmed.
df_meta <- tibble(
  var = names(df_og),
  description = NA_character_)

# The plant number is not a globally unique identifier in this dataset.
# Use site + population + quadrat + plant as the provisional individual ID.
df_og <- df_og %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(str_sub(date, 1, 4)),
    month = as.numeric(str_sub(date, 6, 7)),
    id = str_c(site, pop, qu, plant, sep = '_'),
    record_type = case_when(
      !is.na(s) ~ 'demography',
      is.na(s) & !is.na(burn) ~ 'burn',
      TRUE ~ 'other'))
```

### Initial data structure
```{r}
dim(df_og)
names(df_og)
skimr::skim(df_og)

df_og %>%
  count(record_type)

df_og %>%
  count(year, month)

df_og %>%
  count(site, pop)

df_og %>%
  group_by(site, pop) %>%
  summarise(
    first_year = min(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_year = max(year, na.rm = TRUE),
    nr_quads = n_distinct(qu),
    nr_plants = n_distinct(id), .groups = 'drop')
```

### Separate demographic and burn records
```{r}
# Burn observations are stored as separate rows rather than in the annual
# demographic record. Keep them separate until the fire codes and timing are
# confirmed from the metadata.
df_demog <- df_og %>%
  filter(record_type == 'demography')

df_burn <- df_og %>%
  filter(record_type == 'burn')

# Candidate annual census records. June occurs in every year from 1990-2013,
# but extra demographic censuses also occur in some years and are retained in
# df_demog for now.
df_demog_june <- df_demog %>%
  filter(month == 6)
```


## Sampling inventory
Sampling effort varied among populations and through time. Six populations at
Archbold Biological Station were monitored, with most beginning in 1990 and
population 7 beginning in 1996. A seventh population at Carter Creek was added
in 2001. The number of monitored quadrats also varied among years in several
Archbold populations, whereas the Carter Creek population consisted of 44
quadrats throughout its monitoring period.

Because both the number of quadrats and the duration of monitoring differ among
populations, subsequent analyses retain the population, quadrat, and year
identifiers rather than treating all observations as originating from a single
homogeneous sampling unit.
```{r}
fig_sampling <- df_demog_june %>%
  distinct(site, pop, qu, year) %>%
  mutate(pop_quad = interaction(pop, qu, sep = '-')) %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = year, y = pop_quad)) +
  facet_wrap(~site, scales = 'free_y') +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = 'Sampling inventory', x = 'Year', y = 'Population-quadrat') +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 5)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)) +
  theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 8))
fig_sampling

# ggsave(file.path(dir_result, '0_sampling_inventory.png'),
#        plot = fig_sampling, width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300)
```

## Exploration
No duplicate demographic or fire observations were found for the same
individual and date. Inspection of the original status and stage codes also
shows that the dataset explicitly distinguishes active plants, dormant plants,
missing plants, newly observed plants, and individuals associated with
discontinued monitoring. These distinctions are retained during construction
of the annual demographic histories because absence from an annual census
cannot automatically be interpreted as mortality.
### Exploring identifiers and duplicates
```{r}
# Plant tag numbers are reused among quadrats/populations.
df_og %>%
  distinct(site, pop, qu, plant) %>%
  count(plant, name = 'nr_ids') %>%
  filter(nr_ids > 1) %>%
  arrange(desc(nr_ids), plant)

# Check for duplicate demographic records within individual and date.
df_demog %>%
  group_by(id, date) %>%
  mutate(n_entries = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n_entries > 1) %>%
  arrange(id, date)

# Check for duplicate burn records within individual and date.
df_burn %>%
  group_by(id, date) %>%
  mutate(n_entries = n()) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(n_entries > 1) %>%
  arrange(id, date)
```

### Explore coding before building transitions
```{r}
# Do not convert these codes into survival, recruitment, dormancy or fire
# variables until their exact definitions have been confirmed.
df_demog %>%
  count(s, stage, sort = TRUE)

df_demog %>%
  count(stage, sort = TRUE)

df_demog %>%
  count(s, sort = TRUE)

df_burn %>%
  count(date, site, pop, burn, sort = TRUE)

df_burn %>%
  group_by(date, site, pop, qu) %>%
  summarise(
    nr_records = n(),
    nr_burn_codes = n_distinct(burn),
    burn_codes = paste(sort(unique(burn)), collapse = ', '),
    .groups = 'drop') %>%
  arrange(date, site, pop, qu)
```

## Clean annual demographic history
Individuals of this species can remain belowground and subsequently reappear.
Consequently, an observation coded as absent cannot necessarily be interpreted
as death if the same individual is observed alive again later. We therefore
back-correct records coded as absent or previously absent to dormant when they
occur between two years in which the individual is definitely known to be
alive.

This procedure reclassified 33 annual observations as dormant: 13 originally
coded as absent and 20 originally coded as previously absent. The correction is
deliberately conservative and is made only when later aboveground observation
demonstrates that the individual had not died.
```{r}
# Annual demographic records are the June censuses. Plants recorded as absent
# or previously absent are back-corrected to dormant when they occur between
# two observations where the individual is known to be alive.

df_alive_range <- df_demog_june %>%
  filter(s %in% c(1, 3, 5)) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    first_alive = min(year),
    last_alive = max(year), .groups = "drop")

df_annual <- df_demog_june %>%
  left_join(df_alive_range, by = "id") %>%
  mutate(
    dormancy_repair = s %in% c(0, 9) &
      !is.na(first_alive) & year > first_alive & year < last_alive,
    s_clean = if_else(dormancy_repair, 8, s),
    stage_clean = if_else(dormancy_repair, 5, stage),
    state_clean = case_when(
      s_clean %in% c(1, 3, 5) ~ "active",
      s_clean == 8 ~ "dormant",
      s_clean == 10 ~ "alive_or_dormant",
      s_clean == 0 ~ "absent",
      s_clean == 9 ~ "previous_absent",
      s_clean %in% c(2, 6, 7) ~ "missing",
      s_clean == 11 ~ "discontinued",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_))

# Check repaired dormancy records
df_annual %>%
  filter(dormancy_repair) %>%
  count(s, s_clean)

df_dormancy_check <- df_annual %>%
  filter(any(dormancy_repair), .by = id) %>%
  select(
    site, pop, qu, plant, id, year, s, stage, s_clean, stage_clean,
    state_clean, dia, scape, comment) %>%
  arrange(id, year)

df_dormancy_check
```

## Dormancy duration
Continuous runs of dormant observations were treated as separate dormancy
spells. An individual can therefore contribute more than one spell if it
reappeared aboveground and subsequently entered dormancy again.
```{r}
# Each continuous dormant period is treated as one independent dormancy spell.
# Individuals can therefore contribute more than one dormancy period.

df_dormancy_spell <- df_annual %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    new_spell = row_number() == 1 |
      coalesce(state_clean != lag(state_clean), TRUE) |
      coalesce(year != lag(year) + 1, TRUE),
    spell = cumsum(new_spell)) %>%
  group_by(id, spell) %>%
  summarise(
    state = first(state_clean),
    start_year = min(year),
    end_year = max(year),
    dormancy_years = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(state == "dormant")
```

### Dormancy summary
A total of 409 dormancy spells were identified among 344 individuals. Dormancy
was generally short: the median duration was one year and the mean duration was
1.51 years. Nevertheless, occasional substantially longer periods occurred,
with the longest reconstructed dormant interval lasting 20 years.
```{r}
df_dormancy_summary <- df_dormancy_spell %>%
  summarise(
    n_spells = n(),
    n_individuals = n_distinct(id),
    mean_dormancy = mean(dormancy_years),
    median_dormancy = median(dormancy_years),
    sd_dormancy = sd(dormancy_years),
    min_dormancy = min(dormancy_years),
    max_dormancy = max(dormancy_years))

df_dormancy_summary
```

### Dormancy duration distribution
Most dormant periods were concentrated at short durations. Of the 409 observed
spells, 313 (76.5%) lasted one year, 370 (90.5%) lasted no more than two years,
and 388 (94.9%) lasted no more than three years. Longer dormant periods were
progressively uncommon.
```{r}
df_dormancy_distribution <- df_dormancy_spell %>%
  count(dormancy_years, name = "n_spells") %>%
  arrange(dormancy_years) %>%
  mutate(
    prop = n_spells / sum(n_spells),
    cum_prop = cumsum(prop),
    cum_percent = 100 * cum_prop)

df_dormancy_distribution
```

### Three-year dormancy cutoff
We therefore use three years as an operational threshold when distinguishing
short unresolved absences from mortality. This threshold captures 388 of the
409 observed dormancy spells (94.9%). It should not be interpreted as a
biological maximum for dormancy; rather, it provides a pragmatic rule for
classifying otherwise unresolved absences while accommodating nearly 95% of
the observed dormancy distribution.
```{r}
# The 3-year cutoff is an operational assumption, 
# justified because 388/409 = 94.87% of observed dormancy spells lasted ≤3 years

dormancy_cutoff <- 3

df_dormancy_cutoff <- df_dormancy_spell %>%
  summarise(
    cutoff_years = dormancy_cutoff,
    n_spells = n(),
    n_within_cutoff = sum(dormancy_years <= dormancy_cutoff),
    prop_within_cutoff =
      mean(dormancy_years <= dormancy_cutoff),
    percent_within_cutoff =
      100 * mean(dormancy_years <= dormancy_cutoff))

df_dormancy_cutoff
```

## Annual demographic transitions
Annual demographic transitions are constructed between consecutive June
censuses. Transitions are retained only when observations occur in consecutive
years. Plant size at time \(t\) is defined only for active plants, and growth
between \(t\) and \(t+1\) is defined only for active plants that remain active
at the following census.
```{r}
df_transition <- df_annual %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = lead(year),
    annual_transition = coalesce(year_t1 == year + 1, FALSE),
    s_t1 = if_else(annual_transition, lead(s_clean), NA_real_),
    stage_t1 = if_else(annual_transition, lead(stage_clean), NA_real_),
    state_t1 = if_else(
      annual_transition, lead(state_clean), NA_character_),
    size_t0 = if_else(state_clean == "active", dia, NA_real_),
    size_t1 = if_else(
      annual_transition & state_clean == "active" &
        lead(state_clean) == "active",
      lead(dia), NA_real_),
    size_reactivate_t1 = if_else(
      annual_transition & state_clean == "dormant" &
        lead(state_clean) == "active",
      lead(dia), NA_real_)) %>%
    ungroup()
```

### Check annual state transitions
The annual histories contain 13,804 active-to-active transitions and 406
active-to-dormant transitions. Dormant individuals subsequently returned
aboveground in 409 transitions, while 209 transitions represented continued
dormancy. The remaining transitions include absences, missing observations,
and discontinued monitoring and therefore require additional treatment before
they can be interpreted as survival or mortality.
The annual histories contain 13,804 active-to-active transitions and 406
active-to-dormant transitions. Dormant individuals subsequently returned
aboveground in 409 transitions, while 209 transitions represented continued
dormancy. The remaining transitions include absences, missing observations,
and discontinued monitoring and therefore require additional treatment before
they can be interpreted as survival or mortality.
```{r}
df_transition %>%
  filter(annual_transition) %>%
  count(state_clean, state_t1) |> 
  print(n=100)

df_transition %>%
  filter(
    annual_transition,
    state_clean == "active",
    state_t1 != "active") %>%
  count(year, state_t1) |> 
  print(n=100)
```

### Unresolved absence periods
Periods coded as absent or previously absent were grouped into continuous
absence spells. Their duration is used together with the three-year dormancy
threshold to avoid assigning mortality immediately when a previously active
plant disappears from the census.
```{r}
df_absence_spell <- df_annual %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    absent_state =
      state_clean %in% c("absent", "previous_absent"),
    new_spell = row_number() == 1 |
      coalesce(absent_state != lag(absent_state), TRUE) |
      coalesce(year != lag(year) + 1, TRUE),
    spell = cumsum(new_spell)) %>%
  group_by(id, spell) %>%
  summarise(
    absent_state = first(absent_state),
    absence_start = min(year),
    absence_end = max(year),
    absence_years = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(absent_state)

df_absence_t1 <- df_absence_spell %>%
  transmute(
    id,
    year_t1 = absence_start,
    absence_years)
```

### Demographic outcomes
For individuals beginning a transition either active or dormant, survival is
considered known only when the subsequent observations allow an unambiguous
classification. This produced 14,228 known surviving transitions from active
plants and 873 transitions classified as mortality. An additional 1,191 active
observations remain unresolved and are retained as missing survival outcomes
rather than being forced into either category.

All 618 annual transitions originating from plants classified as dormant that
could be resolved were treated as surviving transitions. This reflects the
retrospective nature of dormancy classification: a dormant state can generally
be confirmed only when the individual is subsequently observed again.
```{r}
df_transition <- df_transition %>%
  left_join(df_absence_t1, by = c("id", "year_t1")) %>%
  mutate(
    survives = case_when(
      !annual_transition ~ NA_real_,
      !state_clean %in% c("active", "dormant") ~ NA_real_,
      state_t1 %in%
        c("active", "dormant", "alive_or_dormant") ~ 1,
      state_t1 %in% c("absent", "previous_absent") &
        absence_years > dormancy_cutoff ~ 0,
      state_t1 %in% c("absent", "previous_absent") &
        absence_years <= dormancy_cutoff ~ NA_real_,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_))

df_transition %>%
  filter(state_clean %in% c("active", "dormant")) %>%
  count(state_clean, survives)

df_transition %>%
  filter(state_clean %in% c("active", "dormant")) %>%
  count(state_clean, survives)
```

### Active and dormant transitions
Among surviving active plants, 406 entered dormancy and 13,804 remained active.
Among dormant plants with resolvable subsequent states, 409 returned to an
active aboveground state and 209 remained dormant. These transitions are kept
explicitly because dormancy represents a discrete demographic state in addition
to the continuous size structure of active plants.
```{r}
df_transition <- df_transition %>%
  mutate(
    enter_dormancy = case_when(
      state_clean != "active" | survives != 1 ~ NA_real_,
      state_t1 == "dormant" ~ 1,
      state_t1 == "active" ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    
    reactivate = case_when(
      state_clean != "dormant" ~ NA_real_,
      state_t1 == "active" ~ 1,
      state_t1 == "dormant" ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_))

df_transition %>%
  count(enter_dormancy)

df_transition %>%
  count(reactivate)
```

## Growth and flowering
For active plants, basal rosette diameter is used as the continuous size
variable. Flowering is identified directly from the recorded number of scapes:
plants with one or more scapes are classified as flowering and plants with zero
scapes as non-flowering. This avoids relying solely on the categorical stage
variable when direct reproductive observations are available.
### Check flowering classification
The categorical stage and scape observations agree almost completely. There
were 2,048 observations classified as flowering stage with one or more scapes.
Only one additional active observation had a positive scape count despite an
ambiguous stage classification. We therefore use the direct scape measurement
to define flowering status.
```{r}
df_annual %>%
  filter(state_clean == "active") %>%
  count(stage_clean, scape > 0, is.na(scape))

df_annual %>%
  filter(
    state_clean == "active",
    (stage_clean == 4 & (scape == 0 | is.na(scape))) |
      (stage_clean != 4 & scape > 0)) %>%
  select(
    site, pop, qu, plant, id, year, s_clean, stage_clean, dia, scape) %>%
  arrange(id, year)

df_transition %>%
  summarise(
    n_active_active = sum(
      state_clean == "active" & state_t1 == "active", na.rm = TRUE),
    n_growth = sum(
      state_clean == "active" & state_t1 == "active" &
        !is.na(size_t0) & !is.na(size_t1), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_missing_growth = sum(
      state_clean == "active" & state_t1 == "active" &
        (is.na(size_t0) | is.na(size_t1)), na.rm = TRUE))
```

### Construct growth and flowering variables
Across the annual demographic histories, 13,804 transitions occurred from an
active plant to an active plant in the following year. Complete diameter
measurements at both censuses were available for 13,628 of these transitions
and form the candidate data for the continuous growth model.

Among active observations, 2,049 were classified as flowering and 13,969 as
non-flowering; 274 active observations lacked sufficient scape information for
flowering to be classified. Plant diameter is log-transformed for subsequent
vital-rate modeling, and quadratic and cubic terms are retained to allow
nonlinear size dependence to be evaluated.
```{r}
df_transition <- df_transition %>%
  mutate(
    flower = case_when(
      state_clean != "active" ~ NA_real_,
      !is.na(scape) & scape > 0 ~ 1,
      !is.na(scape) & scape == 0 ~ 0,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    fl_nr = if_else(state_clean == "active", scape, NA_real_),
    logsize_t0 = log(size_t0),
    logsize_t1 = log(size_t1),
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3)

df_transition %>%
  filter(
    state_clean == "active",
    state_t1 == "active",
    !is.na(size_t0),
    !is.na(size_t1)) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    min_t0 = min(size_t0),
    max_t0 = max(size_t0),
    min_t1 = min(size_t1),
    max_t1 = max(size_t1),
    mean_t0 = mean(size_t0),
    mean_t1 = mean(size_t1))

df_transition %>%
  filter(state_clean == "active") %>%
  count(flower)
```

## Recruitment structure
Recruitment requires a different reconstruction from the other vital rates
because newly encountered plants cannot always be assigned directly to the
preceding year's reproductive cohort. New seedlings are explicitly coded in
the field, whereas some newly encountered larger plants may represent seedlings
that were missed during their first year.

The first observation of each newly recorded individual is therefore identified
using all demographic censuses, including the additional 1998 and 2001
censuses. Observations from censuses occurring after June are assigned to the
following annual recruitment census where appropriate.

A total of 1,268 newly observed plants were identified after excluding
individuals already present when their quadrat first entered the monitoring
program. Of these, 110 were explicitly recorded as seedlings and 1,158 were
recorded as new adults. Baseline individuals are excluded from recruitment
because their actual year of establishment is unknown.
```{r}
df_quad_start <- df_demog_june %>%
  group_by(site, pop, qu) %>%
  summarise(first_quad_year = min(year), .groups = "drop")

df_recruit_first <- df_demog %>%
  filter(s %in% c(3, 5)) %>%
  arrange(id, year, month) %>%
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    recruit_year = if_else(month > 6, year + 1, year)) %>%
  left_join(
    df_quad_start,
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu")) %>%
  mutate(
    baseline = recruit_year == first_quad_year,
    recruit_type = case_when(
      s == 5 ~ "seedling",
      s == 3 ~ "new_adult"))

df_recruit_first %>%
  count(baseline, recruit_type)

df_recruit_first %>%
  filter(!baseline) %>%
  count(recruit_year, recruit_type)

df_recruit_first %>%
  filter(!baseline) %>%
  count(month, recruit_type)
```

### Recruitment size structure
The field classifications are retained rather than replacing them with a
diameter-based rule. Almost all seedlings had diameters no greater than 2 cm,
and almost all new adults were larger than 2 cm, but four observations did not
follow this pattern. In each of these cases the categorical stage information
supports the original field classification, so these records are not
reclassified based on diameter alone.
```{r}
df_recruit_first %>%
  filter(!baseline) %>%
  mutate(
    size_class = case_when(
      is.na(dia) ~ "missing",
      dia <= 2 ~ "<=2 cm",
      dia > 2 ~ ">2 cm")) %>%
  count(recruit_type, size_class)

df_recruit_first %>%
  filter(!baseline) %>%
  group_by(recruit_type, month) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_dia_na = sum(is.na(dia)),
    mean_dia = mean(dia, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_dia = median(dia, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_dia = if (all(is.na(dia))) NA_real_ else min(dia, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_dia = if (all(is.na(dia))) NA_real_ else max(dia, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")
```

### Recruitment classification
Not all newly observed adults are treated as presumed two-year-old recruits.
Following the logic of Satterthwaite et al. (2002), this category is restricted
to newly observed adults entering the annual census as small, stage-2 plants.
Larger newly observed adults cannot be assigned confidently to a particular
previous reproductive cohort and are therefore excluded from the reconstructed
fecundity response.

This classification produced 110 observed seedlings, 396 presumed two-year-old
plants, and 762 other newly observed adults. Observed seedlings are assigned to
the preceding fecundity year, whereas presumed two-year-old plants are assigned
two years backward to the reproductive cohort that could have produced them.
```{r}
df_recruit_entry <- df_recruit_first %>%
  filter(!baseline) %>%
  left_join(
    df_demog_june %>%
      select(
        id, year, s_entry = s, stage_entry = stage,
        dia_entry = dia),
    by = c("id", "recruit_year" = "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    recruit_class = case_when(
      recruit_type == "seedling" ~ "observed_seedling",
      recruit_type == "new_adult" & stage_entry == 2 ~ "presumed_2yr",
      recruit_type == "new_adult" ~ "new_adult_other"),
    fecundity_year = case_when(
      recruit_class == "observed_seedling" ~ recruit_year - 1,
      recruit_class == "presumed_2yr" ~ recruit_year - 2,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_))

df_recruit_entry %>%
  count(recruit_class)

df_recruit_entry %>%
  filter(!is.na(fecundity_year)) %>%
  anti_join(
    df_demog_june %>%
      distinct(site, pop, qu, year),
    by = c(
      "site", "pop", "qu",
      "fecundity_year" = "year")) %>%
  count(recruit_class, fecundity_year)
```

### Recruitment observations usable for fecundity
Recruitment observations are used only when the corresponding fecundity year
was itself monitored in the same quadrat. All 110 observed seedlings could be
assigned to an observed fecundity year. Of the 396 presumed two-year-old
plants, 382 could be assigned, whereas 14 originated from cohorts predating
monitoring of the relevant quadrat and were excluded from fecundity estimation.
```{r}
df_recruit_entry <- df_recruit_entry %>%
  left_join(
    df_demog_june %>%
      distinct(site, pop, qu, year) %>%
      mutate(fecundity_observed = TRUE),
    by = c(
      "site", "pop", "qu",
      "fecundity_year" = "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    fecundity_usable = case_when(
      recruit_class == "new_adult_other" ~ FALSE,
      !is.na(fecundity_year) &
        replace_na(fecundity_observed, FALSE) ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE))

df_recruit_entry %>%
  count(recruit_class, fecundity_usable)
```

### Quadrat monitoring history
Recruitment is modeled at the quadrat rather than individual level because the
parental identity of recruits is unknown. A quadrat-year is considered
monitored only while demographic monitoring of that quadrat remains active.
This prevents years following discontinuation of a quadrat from being
mistakenly interpreted as years with zero recruitment.
```{r}
df_quad_monitor <- df_annual %>%
  group_by(site, pop, qu, year) %>%
  summarise(
    monitored = any(state_clean != "discontinued", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(monitored) %>%
  select(-monitored)
```

### Recruitment follow-up availability
The two reconstructed recruitment components require different amounts of
follow-up. Directly observed seedlings require monitoring through \(t+1\),
whereas presumed two-year-old recruits require monitoring through \(t+2\).
Consequently, an unobserved future cohort is treated as unknown rather than as
zero recruitment.

The resulting recruitment dataset contains 1,371 monitored quadrat-years.
Complete two-year follow-up is available for 1,187 of these observations.
Ninety-two quadrat-years lack the \(t+1\) census and therefore have unknown
seedling recruitment, while 184 lack the full \(t+2\) follow-up required to
estimate presumed two-year-old recruitment. These observations are retained
but coded as missing rather than zero.
```{r}
df_recruit_followup <- df_quad_monitor %>%
  left_join(
    df_quad_monitor %>%
      transmute(
        site, pop, qu,
        year = year - 1,
        monitored_t1 = TRUE),
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_quad_monitor %>%
      transmute(
        site, pop, qu,
        year = year - 2,
        monitored_t2 = TRUE),
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    monitored_t1 = replace_na(monitored_t1, FALSE),
    monitored_t2 = replace_na(monitored_t2, FALSE))
```

### Recruitment counts by fecundity year
```{r}
df_recruit_count <- df_recruit_entry %>%
  filter(fecundity_usable) %>%
  count(
    site, pop, qu, fecundity_year, recruit_class,
    name = "nr_recruits") %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = recruit_class,
    values_from = nr_recruits,
    values_fill = 0)
```

### Simple recruitment counts
```{r}
# For the simple mean IPM, all newly observed adults are assumed to have been
# missed recruits from the preceding annual census.

df_recruit_count_simple <- df_recruit_first %>%
  filter(!baseline) %>%
  mutate(
    fecundity_year_simple = case_when(
      recruit_type == "seedling" ~ recruit_year - 1,
      recruit_type == "new_adult" ~ recruit_year - 2)) %>%
  semi_join(
    df_quad_monitor,
    by = c(
      "site", "pop", "qu",
      "fecundity_year_simple" = "year")) %>%
  count(
    site, pop, qu, fecundity_year_simple, recruit_type,
    name = "nr_recruits") %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = recruit_type,
    values_from = nr_recruits,
    values_fill = 0) %>%
  rename(
    observed_seedling_simple = seedling,
    new_adult_simple = new_adult)
```

### Recruitment working structure
```{r}
df_recruit_quad <- df_recruit_followup %>%
  left_join(
    df_recruit_count,
    by = c(
      "site", "pop", "qu",
      "year" = "fecundity_year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_recruit_count_simple,
    by = c(
      "site", "pop", "qu",
      "year" = "fecundity_year_simple")) %>%
  mutate(
    observed_seedling = case_when(
      monitored_t1 ~ replace_na(observed_seedling, 0L),
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_),
    presumed_2yr = case_when(
      monitored_t2 ~ replace_na(presumed_2yr, 0L),
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_),
    observed_seedling_simple = case_when(
      monitored_t1 ~ replace_na(observed_seedling_simple, 0L),
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_),
    new_adult_simple = case_when(
      monitored_t2 ~ replace_na(new_adult_simple, 0L),
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_),
    recruitment_complete = monitored_t1 & monitored_t2,
    nr_recruit = case_when(
      recruitment_complete ~ observed_seedling + presumed_2yr,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_),
    recruits_simple = case_when(
      recruitment_complete ~
        observed_seedling_simple + new_adult_simple,
      TRUE ~ NA_integer_))

df_recruit_quad %>%
  count(year, monitored_t1, monitored_t2) %>%
  print(n = 100)

df_recruit_quad %>%
  summarise(
    n_quad_years = n(),
    n_complete = sum(recruitment_complete),
    n_incomplete = sum(!recruitment_complete),
    n_seedling_unknown = sum(is.na(observed_seedling)),
    n_presumed_unknown = sum(is.na(presumed_2yr)))
```

### Parental reproductive abundance
Potential parental reproductive abundance is summarized for each monitored
quadrat and year. We retain the number of active plants, flowering plants, and
flowering scapes. Quadrat-years with no active plants are genuine reproductive
zeros, whereas quadrat-years containing active plants but no usable scape
observations are treated as unknown.

Of the 1,371 monitored quadrat-years, 32 contained no active plants and 10 had
insufficient information to determine flowering or scape abundance.
```{r}
df_repro_quad <- df_quad_monitor %>%
  left_join(
    df_annual %>%
      filter(state_clean != "discontinued") %>%
      group_by(site, pop, qu, year) %>%
      summarise(
        nr_active = sum(state_clean == "active", na.rm = TRUE),
        nr_flower_obs = sum(
          state_clean == "active" & !is.na(scape), na.rm = TRUE),
        flowering_sum = sum(
          state_clean == "active" & scape > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
        scape_sum = sum(
          if_else(state_clean == "active", scape, NA_real_),
          na.rm = TRUE),
        nr_invol_obs = sum(
          state_clean == "active" & !is.na(invol), na.rm = TRUE),
        invol_sum = sum(
          if_else(state_clean == "active", invol, NA_real_),
          na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
      mutate(
        nr_flowering = case_when(
          nr_active == 0 ~ 0,
          nr_flower_obs == 0 ~ NA_real_,
          TRUE ~ as.numeric(flowering_sum)),
        nr_scapes = case_when(
          nr_active == 0 ~ 0,
          nr_flower_obs == 0 ~ NA_real_,
          TRUE ~ scape_sum),
        nr_invol = case_when(
          nr_active == 0 ~ 0,
          nr_invol_obs == 0 ~ NA_real_,
          TRUE ~ invol_sum)) %>%
      select(
        site, pop, qu, year, nr_active, nr_flower_obs,
        nr_flowering, nr_scapes, nr_invol_obs, nr_invol),
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year"))
```

### Population-level reproductive abundance
Recruitment may originate from seed produced outside the focal quadrat.
Reproductive abundance is therefore also summarized across the other monitored
quadrats in the same population and across the population as a whole. Both
local and surrounding reproductive abundance are retained in the working data
so that their relative support can be evaluated during recruitment-model
selection rather than imposed during data preparation.
```{r}
df_repro_pop <- df_repro_quad %>%
  group_by(site, pop, year) %>%
  summarise(
    nr_quads = n(),
    nr_active_pop = sum(nr_active),
    nr_quads_flower_obs = sum(!is.na(nr_flowering)),
    nr_flowering_pop_obs = sum(nr_flowering, na.rm = TRUE),
    nr_quads_scape_obs = sum(!is.na(nr_scapes)),
    nr_scapes_pop_obs = sum(nr_scapes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    nr_flowering_pop = if_else(
      nr_quads_flower_obs == nr_quads,
      nr_flowering_pop_obs, NA_real_),
    nr_scapes_pop = if_else(
      nr_quads_scape_obs == nr_quads,
      nr_scapes_pop_obs, NA_real_),
    mean_flowering_pop = if_else(
      nr_quads_flower_obs > 0,
      nr_flowering_pop_obs / nr_quads_flower_obs, NA_real_),
    mean_scapes_pop = if_else(
      nr_quads_scape_obs > 0,
      nr_scapes_pop_obs / nr_quads_scape_obs, NA_real_))
```

### Add reproductive abundance to recruitment data
```{r}
df_recruit_quad <- df_recruit_quad %>%
  left_join(
    df_repro_quad,
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_repro_pop,
    by = c("site", "pop", "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    nr_flowering_other =
      nr_flowering_pop_obs - replace_na(nr_flowering, 0),
    nr_quads_flower_other =
      nr_quads_flower_obs - as.integer(!is.na(nr_flowering)),
    mean_flowering_other = if_else(
      nr_quads_flower_other > 0,
      nr_flowering_other / nr_quads_flower_other, NA_real_),
    nr_scapes_other =
      nr_scapes_pop_obs - replace_na(nr_scapes, 0),
    nr_quads_scape_other =
      nr_quads_scape_obs - as.integer(!is.na(nr_scapes)),
    mean_scapes_other = if_else(
      nr_quads_scape_other > 0,
      nr_scapes_other / nr_quads_scape_other, NA_real_))
```

### Recruitment without local flowering
```{r}
df_recruit_quad %>%
  mutate(nr_recruit = observed_seedling + presumed_2yr) %>%
  filter(nr_recruit > 0) %>%
  count(local_flowering = nr_flowering > 0)
```

### Reproductive data through time
```{r}
df_repro_quad %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    nr_flowering = sum(nr_flowering),
    nr_scapes = sum(nr_scapes, na.rm = TRUE),
    nr_invol_obs = sum(nr_invol_obs),
    .groups = "drop")
```

### Recruitment and flowering at population level
```{r}
df_recruit_pop <- df_recruit_quad %>%
  group_by(site, pop, year) %>%
  summarise(
    observed_seedling = sum(observed_seedling),
    presumed_2yr = sum(presumed_2yr),
    nr_flowering = sum(nr_flowering),
    nr_scapes = sum(nr_scapes, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(nr_recruit = observed_seedling + presumed_2yr)

df_recruit_pop %>%
  filter(nr_recruit > 0, nr_flowering == 0)
```

### Recruitment correction
Because small seedlings can be missed during annual censuses, Satterthwaite et
al. (2002) considered alternative fertility estimates based on presumed
two-year-old plants. We retain analogous pessimistic and optimistic recruitment
measures. The pessimistic estimate counts each presumed two-year-old as one
recruit, whereas the optimistic estimate adjusts this component by estimated
first-year seedling survival.

Observed seedling survival in the present data was 0.728, based on 103
transitions for which survival could be resolved. Among the 1,187 quadrat-years
with complete recruitment follow-up, mean reconstructed recruitment was 0.411
recruits per quadrat-year under the pessimistic estimate and 0.531 under the
survival-corrected optimistic estimate. Maximum values were 22 and 30.2,
respectively.
```{r}
seedling_survival <- df_transition %>%
  filter(stage_clean == 1, !is.na(survives)) %>%
  summarise(seedling_survival = mean(survives)) %>%
  pull(seedling_survival)

df_recruit_quad <- df_recruit_quad %>%
  mutate(
    recruits_pess = if_else(
      recruitment_complete,
      as.numeric(observed_seedling + presumed_2yr), NA_real_),
    recruits_opt = if_else(
      recruitment_complete,
      observed_seedling + presumed_2yr / seedling_survival,
      NA_real_))

df_repro_quad %>%
  summarise(
    n_quad_years = n(),
    n_zero_active = sum(nr_active == 0),
    n_flowering_unknown = sum(is.na(nr_flowering)),
    n_scapes_unknown = sum(is.na(nr_scapes)))

df_recruit_quad %>%
  summarise(
    n_complete = sum(recruitment_complete),
    mean_pess = mean(recruits_pess, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_opt = mean(recruits_opt, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_pess = max(recruits_pess, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_opt = max(recruits_opt, na.rm = TRUE))
```

## Fire-event structure
The dataset contains observations from nine prescribed-fire events between 1998
and 2013. Fire exposure varies substantially within events: some fires affected
all recorded locations in a quadrat, whereas others were spatially patchy.
Consequently, fire is retained both as a binary quadrat-level exposure and as
the proportion of scored locations burned within each quadrat.
```{r}
df_fire <- df_burn %>%
  mutate(
    fire_year = year,
    fire_month = month,
    fire_event = date,
    burned = case_when(
      burn == 0 ~ 0,
      burn %in% c(1, 2, 4) ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    fire_severity = case_when(
      burn == 0 ~ "unburned",
      burn == 1 ~ "scorched",
      burn == 2 ~ "consumed",
      burn == 4 ~ "burned_unspecified",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    transition_year = case_when(
      fire_event == "1998-05" ~ 1997,
      fire_event == "1998-07" ~ 1998,
      fire_event == "2001-08" ~ 2001,
      fire_event == "2002-10" ~ 2002,
      fire_event == "2005-04" ~ 2004,
      fire_event == "2007-12" ~ 2007,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    timing_known = !is.na(transition_year))

df_fire %>%
  count(fire_event, fire_severity)

df_fire %>%
  group_by(fire_event, site, pop, qu) %>%
  summarise(
    nr_scored = n(),
    nr_burned = sum(burned == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_burned = mean(burned, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(fire_event) %>%
  summarise(
    nr_quads = n(),
    min_prop = min(prop_burned),
    mean_prop = mean(prop_burned),
    max_prop = max(prop_burned),
    .groups = "drop")
```

### Fire records relative to demographic observations
Fire records cannot always be interpreted as direct observations of the
demographic response of a living individual. In several events, fire records
exist for plant locations before the corresponding individual first appears in
the demographic dataset. The fire records are therefore interpreted primarily
as spatial information on exposure at marked locations rather than requiring
the associated plant to have been observed alive at the time of the fire.
```{r}
df_first_demog <- df_demog %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    first_demog_date = min(date),
    .groups = "drop")

df_fire_history_check <- df_fire %>%
  left_join(df_first_demog, by = "id") %>%
  mutate(
    fire_time = as.Date(paste0(fire_event, "-01")),
    first_demog_time = as.Date(paste0(first_demog_date, "-01")),
    first_observed_after_fire = first_demog_time > fire_time)

df_fire_history_check %>%
  count(fire_event, first_observed_after_fire)

df_fire_history_check %>%
  filter(fire_event == "2001-08") %>%
  count(first_demog_date)
```

### Quadrat-level fire exposure
Fire exposure was aggregated to the quadrat level using both the occurrence of
any burned records and the proportion of scored records that were burned. This
preserves information on partial burns rather than assigning an entire
population or quadrat to a burn category solely because a fire occurred nearby.
```{r}
df_fire_quad <- df_fire %>%
  group_by(fire_event, site, pop, qu) %>%
  summarise(
    transition_year = first(transition_year),
    timing_known = first(timing_known),
    nr_scored = n(),
    nr_burned = sum(burned == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    nr_unburned = sum(burned == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    prop_burned = mean(burned, na.rm = TRUE),
    any_burned = as.numeric(any(burned == 1, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop")
```

### Fire-event spatial footprint
The extent of burning differed strongly among events. Some events, including
May 1998 and April 2005, burned all scored locations within affected quadrats,
whereas others were highly heterogeneous. This variation supports retaining
quadrat-level fire exposure rather than using only an event- or
population-level indicator.
```{r}
df_fire_quad %>%
  distinct(fire_event, site, pop, timing_known, transition_year) %>%
  arrange(fire_event, site, pop)
```

### Quadrat coverage of known-timing fires
Fire assessment coverage was complete for the known-timing Archbold events.
At Carter Creek, however, only 22 of 44 monitored quadrats were scored following
the 2001 fire and 27 of 44 following the 2007 fire. Unscored quadrats in these
events are therefore retained as unknown fire exposure rather than being
classified as unburned.
```{r}
df_fire_pop <- df_fire_quad %>%
  distinct(
    fire_event, site, pop, transition_year, timing_known)

df_fire_quad_coverage <- df_fire_pop %>%
  filter(timing_known) %>%
  inner_join(
    df_demog_june %>%
      distinct(site, pop, qu, year),
    by = c(
      "site", "pop",
      "transition_year" = "year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_quad %>%
      select(
        fire_event, site, pop, qu,
        prop_burned, any_burned),
    by = c("fire_event", "site", "pop", "qu")) %>%
  mutate(fire_scored = !is.na(prop_burned))

df_fire_quad_coverage %>%
  group_by(fire_event, site, pop) %>%
  summarise(
    nr_quads_monitored = n(),
    nr_quads_scored = sum(fire_scored),
    prop_quads_scored = mean(fire_scored),
    .groups = "drop")

df_fire_quad_coverage %>%
  filter(!fire_scored) %>%
  count(fire_event, site, pop)
```

### Known fire events
For six fire events, the timing relative to the annual June census can be
assigned sufficiently clearly to an annual demographic transition. These
events are linked to the transition beginning in the census year immediately
preceding the fire when appropriate.
```{r}
df_fire_pop_year <- df_fire_quad %>%
  filter(timing_known) %>%
  distinct(fire_event, site, pop, transition_year)
```

### Ambiguous fire timing
The timing of three later fires cannot be resolved confidently relative to the
annual census because the available census information does not provide the
exact within-month ordering required to determine whether the fire preceded or
followed that year's demographic observation. Rather than imposing an
unsupported ordering, both potentially affected annual transitions are flagged
as timing-ambiguous and their fire exposure is set to missing.
```{r}
# For these fires, the annual census could have occurred either before or after
# the fire. Both possible annual transitions are therefore treated as unknown.

df_fire_ambiguous <- df_fire_quad %>%
  filter(!timing_known) %>%
  distinct(fire_event, site, pop) %>%
  mutate(fire_year = as.numeric(str_sub(fire_event, 1, 4))) %>%
  {
    bind_rows(
      transmute(
        ., fire_event, site, pop,
        candidate_year = fire_year - 1),
      transmute(
        ., fire_event, site, pop,
        candidate_year = fire_year))
  }
```

### Annual quadrat fire exposure
```{r}
df_fire_transition_quad <- df_demog_june %>%
  distinct(site, pop, qu, year) %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_pop_year,
    by = c("site", "pop", "year" = "transition_year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_quad %>%
      filter(timing_known) %>%
      select(
        fire_event, site, pop, qu,
        nr_scored, nr_burned, nr_unburned,
        prop_burned, any_burned),
    by = c("fire_event", "site", "pop", "qu")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_ambiguous %>%
      rename(ambiguous_event = fire_event),
    by = c(
      "site", "pop",
      "year" = "candidate_year")) %>%
  mutate(
    timing_ambiguous = !is.na(ambiguous_event),
    fire_event_pop = !is.na(fire_event),
    
    fire_prop_quad = case_when(
      timing_ambiguous ~ NA_real_,
      !fire_event_pop ~ 0,
      !is.na(prop_burned) ~ prop_burned,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    
    dist_transition = case_when(
      timing_ambiguous ~ NA_real_,
      !fire_event_pop ~ 0,
      !is.na(any_burned) ~ any_burned,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_))
```

### Previous annual fire exposure
In addition to current-transition fire exposure, the working data retain
whether the quadrat experienced fire during the preceding annual transition.
This permits demographic responses during the fire interval and responses in
the subsequent year to be estimated separately.
```{r}
df_fire_previous <- df_fire_transition_quad %>%
  transmute(
    site, pop, qu,
    year = year + 1,
    disturbance_prev = dist_transition,
    fire_prop_prev = fire_prop_quad)

df_transition <- df_transition %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_transition_quad %>%
      select(
        site, pop, qu, year,
        fire_event, ambiguous_event, timing_ambiguous,
        dist_transition, fire_prop_quad),
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_previous,
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year"))
```

### Individual fire exposure
Individual-level fire records are retained as supplementary exposure
information. Their coverage is substantially less complete than the
quadrat-level data, particularly for several fire events. Quadrat-level fire
exposure therefore provides the principal consistently available fire
covariate, while individual burn status can be evaluated where it is observed.
```{r}
df_fire_individual <- df_fire %>%
  filter(timing_known) %>%
  select(
    fire_event, id,
    burned_ind = burned,
    fire_severity_ind = fire_severity)

df_transition <- df_transition %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_individual,
    by = c("fire_event", "id")) %>%
  mutate(
    burned_ind = case_when(
      timing_ambiguous ~ NA_real_,
      is.na(fire_event) ~ 0,
      !is.na(burned_ind) ~ burned_ind,
      TRUE ~ NA_real_))
```

### Previous individual fire exposure
```{r}
df_fire_ind_previous <- df_transition %>%
  transmute(
    id,
    year = year + 1,
    burned_ind_prev = burned_ind)

df_transition <- df_transition %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_ind_previous,
    by = c("id", "year"))

df_fire_transition_quad %>%
  count(timing_ambiguous, dist_transition)

df_transition %>%
  filter(!is.na(fire_event)) %>%
  count(fire_event, burned_ind)

df_fire_transition_quad %>%
  filter(!timing_ambiguous, fire_event_pop) %>%
  count(fire_event, is.na(dist_transition))

```

### Check that fire joins did not duplicate demographic records
Joining the reconstructed fire histories to the demographic histories did not
duplicate any individual-year records. The final demographic transition table
contains 33,369 rows and the same number of unique individual-by-year
combinations.
```{r}
df_transition %>%
  count(id, year) %>%
  filter(n > 1)

nrow(df_transition)

df_transition %>%
  distinct(id, year) %>%
  nrow()
```

## Working data
The final working dataset is designed to contain all information required to
construct the subsequent IPM while preserving the observational scale at which
each demographic process was measured. Individual demographic transitions and
quadrat-level recruitment observations are therefore stored as separate row
types within a single data object.

### Recruitment working rows
Recruitment rows represent one monitored quadrat in one fecundity year. They
contain reconstructed recruitment, local and surrounding reproductive
abundance, follow-up completeness, and the corresponding fire history. They do
not represent individual plants.
```{r}
df_recruit <- df_recruit_quad %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_transition_quad %>%
      select(
        site, pop, qu, year, fire_event, ambiguous_event,
        timing_ambiguous, dist_transition, fire_prop_quad),
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_fire_previous,
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  transmute(
    row_type = "recruitment",
    site, pop, qu, year,
    monitored_t1, monitored_t2,
    recruitment_complete,
    observed_seedling_simple, new_adult_simple, recruits_simple,
    observed_seedling, presumed_2yr, nr_recruit,
    recruits_pess, recruits_opt,
    nr_active, nr_flowering, nr_scapes, nr_invol,
    nr_flowering_other, mean_flowering_other,
    nr_scapes_other, mean_scapes_other,
    nr_quads, nr_active_pop,
    nr_flowering_pop, mean_flowering_pop,
    nr_scapes_pop, mean_scapes_pop,
    dist_transition, disturbance_prev,
    fire_prop_quad, fire_prop_prev,
    timing_ambiguous, fire_event, ambiguous_event)
```

### Individual recruitment identity
```{r}
df_recruit_ind <- df_recruit_first %>%
  filter(!baseline) %>%
  transmute(
    id,
    year = recruit_year,
    recruit_type)
```

### Individual working rows
Individual rows represent one plant in one annual census year and contain the
variables required for survival, continuous growth, flowering, dormancy,
reactivation, and fire-response models.
```{r}
df_ind <- df_transition %>%
  left_join(
    df_recruit_ind,
    by = c("id", "year")) %>%
  transmute(
    row_type = "individual",
    site, pop, qu, plant, id, year,
    state = state_clean,
    state_t1,
    stage = stage_clean,
    stage_t1,
    survives,
    enter_dormancy,
    recruit_type,
    size_reactivate_t1,
    reactivate,
    size_t0,
    size_t1,
    logsize_t0,
    logsize_t1,
    logsize_t0_2,
    logsize_t0_3,
    flower,
    fl_nr,
    invol,
    herb,
    dist_transition,
    disturbance_prev,
    fire_prop_quad,
    fire_prop_prev,
    burned_ind,
    burned_ind_prev,
    fire_severity_ind,
    timing_ambiguous,
    fire_event,
    ambiguous_event)
```

### Combine working data
The two observational scales are combined by stacking, rather than joining,
the individual and recruitment records. This is important because joining
quadrat-level recruitment onto individual plants would repeat the same
recruitment response once for every plant in the quadrat and create
pseudoreplication. The `row_type` variable therefore identifies whether a row
contains an individual demographic observation or a quadrat-level recruitment
observation.
```{r}
# The final working data contain both individual demographic observations and
# quadrat-level recruitment observations. Recruitment is kept as separate rows
# rather than repeated for every individual within a quadrat.

df <- bind_rows(
  df_ind,
  df_recruit) %>%
  mutate(
    row_type = factor(row_type),
    year = as.numeric(year),
    site = factor(site),
    pop = factor(pop),
    state = factor(state),
    state_t1 = factor(state_t1),
    stage = factor(stage),
    stage_t1 = factor(stage_t1))
```

### Final working-data checks
Final integrity checks confirm that individual rows remain unique by individual
and year and that recruitment rows remain unique by site, population, quadrat,
and year. Continuous growth is restricted to active-to-active transitions,
dormancy entry occurs only from active plants, and reactivation occurs only
from dormant plants. Fire exposure for transitions with unresolved fire timing
also remains explicitly missing.

The resulting working data can therefore be used as the single input dataset
for the subsequent IPM analyses while retaining the distinct observational
structure of the individual and recruitment vital rates.
```{r}
df %>%
  count(row_type)

stopifnot(
  df %>%
    filter(row_type == "individual") %>%
    nrow() ==
    df %>%
    filter(row_type == "individual") %>%
    distinct(id, year) %>%
    nrow(),
  
  df %>%
    filter(row_type == "recruitment") %>%
    nrow() ==
    df %>%
    filter(row_type == "recruitment") %>%
    distinct(site, pop, qu, year) %>%
    nrow())

# Check individual vital-rate structure
df %>%
  filter(row_type == "individual") %>%
  count(state, survives)

df %>%
  filter(
    row_type == "individual",
    !is.na(size_t1)) %>%
  count(state, state_t1)

df %>%
  filter(
    row_type == "individual",
    !is.na(enter_dormancy)) %>%
  count(state, state_t1, enter_dormancy)

df %>%
  filter(
    row_type == "individual",
    !is.na(reactivate)) %>%
  count(state, state_t1, reactivate)

# Check recruitment structure
df %>%
  filter(row_type == "recruitment") %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_complete = sum(recruitment_complete),
    n_pess = sum(!is.na(recruits_pess)),
    n_opt = sum(!is.na(recruits_opt)))

# Check ambiguous fire transitions
df %>%
  filter(timing_ambiguous) %>%
  count(row_type, dist_transition, fire_prop_quad)
```

# Mean IPM {#ipm_mean}

## Introduction

This analysis develops a mean integral projection model (IPM) for
*Eriogonum longifolium* var. *gnaphalifolium* using the long-term demographic
data from Archbold Biological Station and Carter Creek. The purpose of this
first IPM is to provide a relatively simple description of the principal
demographic processes and their consequences for long-term population growth.
Vital rates are therefore pooled across years, populations, and disturbance
histories rather than allowing demographic relationships to vary through time
or among sites. The resulting kernel represents the demographic conditions
averaged across the observations contained in the dataset and should not be
interpreted specifically as an unburned or post-fire kernel.

The population is represented by two demographic states. Above-ground plants
are described continuously by log-transformed basal rosette diameter, whereas
dormant plants form one additional discrete state. With 200 continuous size
classes, the complete projection kernel therefore contains 201 states. This
structure retains the principal advantage of an IPM, namely continuous
size-dependent demographic rates, while explicitly accommodating prolonged
below-ground dormancy, which is an important feature of the life history of
*E. longifolium* var. *gnaphalifolium*.

The mean kernel can be written conceptually as

$$
\mathbf{K} =
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{T} + \mathbf{F} & \mathbf{R} \\
\mathbf{D}              & P_{DD}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where $\mathbf{T}$ describes survival and growth of active plants,
$\mathbf{F}$ describes recruitment from active plants, $\mathbf{D}$ describes
entry into dormancy, $\mathbf{R}$ describes reactivation into the continuous
active-size distribution, and $P_{DD}$ is the probability that a dormant plant
remains dormant.

### Survival, growth, and entry into dormancy

Survival is modeled for plants that are active at census $t$. Candidate
binomial models contain an intercept and linear, quadratic, or cubic functions
of log basal diameter, with model complexity selected using AICc. Survival
includes plants that remain active as well as plants that subsequently enter
dormancy. Consequently, dormancy is not treated as mortality.

Growth is estimated only from transitions in which a plant is active at both
$t$ and $t+1$. Log diameter at $t+1$ is modeled as an intercept, linear,
quadratic, or cubic function of log diameter at $t$, again with model
complexity selected by AICc. Growth variance is heteroscedastic. Squared
residuals from the selected growth model are modeled as an exponential
function of the fitted growth mean, so that the standard deviation used in the
growth kernel varies with expected size at $t+1$.

Entry into dormancy is estimated separately for active plants known to have
survived the annual transition. A binomial model describes the conditional
probability that a surviving active individual enters dormancy as a function
of its size. This conditional formulation is important for the construction of
the kernel. For an active plant of size $x$, the probability of remaining in
the continuous active state is

$$
S(x)[1-D(x)],
$$

where $S(x)$ is survival and $D(x)$ is the probability of entering dormancy
conditional on survival. The probability of moving from the active state into
the dormant state is correspondingly

$$
S(x)D(x).
$$

Thus, survival is first allocated between active and dormant destinations
rather than dormancy being modeled as an additional loss from the population.

### Dormancy and reactivation

Dormant plants have no observable above-ground size, so their subsequent
reactivation cannot be modeled as a function of current size. Reactivation is
therefore represented by an intercept-only binomial model that estimates one
mean annual probability of returning to the active state. Plants that
reactivate are distributed across the continuous size axis according to the
observed log-diameter distribution of plants when they reappear above ground.

No independent mortality probability is estimated for the dormant state in
this first mean IPM. A dormant individual therefore either reactivates with
probability $p_R$ or remains dormant with probability $1-p_R$. The dormant
column of the kernel consequently sums to one. This is a simplifying
assumption arising from the difficulty of distinguishing mortality during
dormancy from continued unobserved dormancy in the census data.

### Flowering and flowering-scape production

Reproduction is divided into two sequential vital rates. First, the
probability that an active individual flowers is modeled with a binomial
regression as a function of log diameter. Second, among flowering individuals,
the number of flowering scapes is modeled using a negative-binomial
regression. Intercept-only, linear, quadratic, and cubic size relationships
are considered for both components where appropriate and selected using AICc.

The expected number of flowering scapes produced by an active individual of
size $x$ is therefore

$$
P_F(x)N_F(x),
$$

where $P_F(x)$ is its probability of flowering and $N_F(x)$ is its expected
number of scapes conditional on flowering. This decomposition avoids treating
the large number of non-flowering individuals as structural zeros in the
scape-number model.

### Recruitment

Recruitment requires additional assumptions because newly observed plants
cannot always be assigned unambiguously to a particular reproductive event.
Observed seedlings are treated directly as recruits. In addition, for this
simple mean IPM, all post-baseline individuals first observed as new adults
are assumed to have been seedlings that were missed during the preceding
census. These individuals are therefore back-assigned to the preceding
recruitment cohort. This follows the general rationale used previously for
presumed two-year-old plants in this species, but represents a deliberately
inclusive recruitment assumption.

Recruitment abundance is related to flowering-scape abundance at the
population-year level using a negative-binomial model. The selected model
allows expected recruitment to increase sublinearly with the number of
contemporaneous flowering scapes,

$$
\log E(R) =
\beta_0 +
\beta_1\log(1 + N_{\mathrm{scape}}).
$$

The non-zero intercept allows recruitment to occur even when no flowering
scapes are recorded in the current census. It should therefore be interpreted
as recruitment not explained by contemporaneous observed flowering, which may
include reproductive carry-over, incomplete observation of reproductive
output, dispersal, or other unmeasured processes.

This population-level recruitment relationship cannot be inserted directly
into a conventional linear individual-based IPM because it contains both an
intercept and a nonlinear dependence on total population-level scape
abundance. For the mean IPM, the fitted recruitment relationship is therefore
collapsed to a single overall fitted recruit-to-scape conversion. This scalar
is used only to construct the linear fertility kernel and represents an
average conversion over the demographic conditions observed in the dataset.

The size distribution of recruits is estimated separately using individuals
actually observed as seedlings. New adults contribute to reconstructed
recruit abundance but do not determine the recruit-size distribution. All
recruits entering the IPM are consequently distributed across the continuous
size axis according to the observed log-diameter distribution of true
seedlings.

### Fertility and construction of the complete kernel

For an active individual of size $x$, the fertility contribution to recruits
of size $y$ is

$$
F(y,x) =
P_F(x)
N_F(x)
c_R
f_R(y),
$$

where $c_R$ is the mean fitted recruitment conversion and $f_R(y)$ is the
recruit-size distribution. Fertility is not multiplied by survival because
reproduction during the census interval can contribute recruits at $t+1$
independently of whether the parent subsequently survives to that census.

The active-to-active transition kernel is

$$
T(y,x) =
S(x)
[1-D(x)]
G(y,x),
$$

where $G(y,x)$ is the size-transition distribution. Growth probabilities that
fall beyond the lower or upper integration limits are returned to the nearest
boundary size class to avoid loss of probability mass through eviction.
Recruit and reactivation size distributions are similarly normalized over the
modeled size interval.

The complete kernel therefore combines continuous active-plant dynamics with
one discrete dormant state. Active individuals may remain active, enter
dormancy, or contribute new recruits; dormant individuals may reactivate into
the continuous size distribution or remain dormant.

Because all vital-rate relationships are pooled across years, the resulting
kernel is a single time-invariant mean kernel. Its dominant eigenvalue is the
asymptotic population growth rate associated with these mean demographic
conditions. The current model gives an asymptotic growth rate of approximately

$$
\lambda = 0.990,
$$

indicating a slowly declining population under the demographic conditions
represented by the mean IPM. This is close to the reconstructed realized
long-term population trajectory, for which the geometric mean annual growth
rate is approximately $0.998$. The two quantities are not expected to be
identical: the first is the asymptotic growth rate of a population subjected
repeatedly to one mean kernel, whereas the second reflects the sequence of
annual population changes actually observed.



## Specifications
### Vital model leaverage
```{r}
v_mod_set_su   <- c()
v_mod_set_gr   <- c()
v_mod_set_do   <- c()
v_mod_set_fl   <- c()
v_mod_set_fl_n <- c()
```

## Data
```{r}
df <- read.csv(
  file.path(
    dir_data,
    paste0("ab_", v_sp_abb, "_df_workdata_260820.csv"))) %>%
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(year),
    row_type = as.character(row_type))

df_ind <- df %>%
  filter(row_type == "individual")

df_re <- df %>%
  filter(
    row_type == "recruitment",
    recruitment_complete,
    !is.na(recruits_simple))
```

## Vital rates
### Survival
#### Data
```{r}
df_su <- df %>%
  filter(
    state == "active",
    !is.na(survives),
    size_t0 > 0,
    is.finite(logsize_t0)) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    id, year, size_t0, survives,
    logsize_t0, logsize_t0_2, logsize_t0_3)
```

#### Model
```{r}
mod_su_0 <- glm(
  survives ~ 1,
  data = df_su, family = "binomial")

mod_su_1 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0,
  data = df_su, family = "binomial")

mod_su_2 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2,
  data = df_su, family = "binomial")

mod_su_3 <- glm(
  survives ~ logsize_t0 + logsize_t0_2 + logsize_t0_3,
  data = df_su, family = "binomial")

mods_su <- list(
  mod_su_0, mod_su_1, mod_su_2, mod_su_3)

mods_su_dAICc <- AICctab(
  mods_su, weights = TRUE, sort = FALSE)$dAICc

mods_su_sorted <- order(mods_su_dAICc)

if (length(v_mod_set_su) == 0) {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- mods_su_sorted[1]
  v_mod_su_index <- mod_su_index_bestfit - 1
} else {
  mod_su_index_bestfit <- v_mod_set_su + 1
  v_mod_su_index <- v_mod_set_su
}

mod_su_bestfit <- mods_su[[mod_su_index_bestfit]]

mod_su_bestfit
mods_su_dAICc
```

#### Plot
```{r}
df_su_newdata <- df_su %>%
  summarise(
    x = list(seq(
      min(logsize_t0),
      max(logsize_t0),
      length.out = 100)),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  unnest(x) %>%
  mutate(
    logsize_t0 = x,
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3) %>%
  mutate(
    predicted = predict(
      mod_su_bestfit,
      newdata = .,
      type = "response"))

fig_su_line <- ggplot(
  df_su,
  aes(x = logsize_t0, y = survives)) +
  geom_jitter(
    height = 0.05, width = 0,
    alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(
    data = df_su_newdata,
    aes(y = predicted),
    linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Survival probability by size",
    subtitle = v_ggp_suffix,
    x = expression("log(diameter)"[t0]),
    y = "Probability of survival") +
  theme_bw()


df_su_bindata <- plot_binned_prop(
  df_su, 10, logsize_t0, survives)

df_su_pred <- df_su %>%
  reframe(
    logsize_t0 = seq(
      min(logsize_t0),
      max(logsize_t0),
      length.out = 100)) %>%
  mutate(
    logsize_t0_2 = logsize_t0^2,
    logsize_t0_3 = logsize_t0^3) %>%
  mutate(
    survives = predict(
      mod_su_bestfit,
      newdata = .,
      type = "response"))

fig_su_bin <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(
    data = df_su_bindata,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, y = survives)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    data = df_su_bindata,
    aes(
      x = logsize_t0,
      ymin = lwr,
      ymax = upr),
    width = 0.1) +
  geom_line(
    data = df_su_pred,
    aes(x = logsize_t0, y = survives),
    linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    x = expression("log(diameter)"[t0]),
    y = "") +
  theme_bw() +
  ylim(0, 1)

fig_su <- fig_su_line + fig_su_bin + plot_layout()
fig_su
```

```{r}

# Squared residuals
mod_gr_y   <- resid(mod_gr_bestfit)^2  
# Non-linear model for variance
mod_gr_var <- nls(
  mod_gr_y ~ a * exp(b * mod_gr_x), start = list(a = 1, b = 0),
  control = nls.control(maxiter = 1000, tol = 1e-6, warnOnly = TRUE))
```

```{r}
mods_re_dAICc
```

#### Mean recruitment conversion for the IPM
```{r}

# recruitment relationship to one mean recruits-per-scape conversion.

df_sc2re_mod <- df_sc2re_mod %>%
  mutate(
    recruits_pred = predict(
      mod_re_bestfit,
      type = "response"))

recr_per_scape <- sum(df_sc2re_mod$recruits_pred) /
```

## Extracting parameter estimates
```{r}
# Survival
coef_su <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_su_bestfit)),
  value = coef(mod_su_bestfit)) %>%
  mutate(
    coefficient = as.character(coefficient),
    coefficient = replace(
      coefficient, grepl("Intercept", coefficient), "b0"))

# Growth
coef_gr_fe <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_gr_bestfit)),
  value = coef(mod_gr_bestfit))

coef_gr_var <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_gr_var)),
  value = coef(mod_gr_var))

coef_gr <- bind_rows(coef_gr_fe, coef_gr_var) %>%
  mutate(
    coefficient = as.character(coefficient),
    coefficient = replace(
      coefficient, grepl("Intercept", coefficient), "b0"))

# Dormancy entry
coef_do <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_do_bestfit)),
  value = coef(mod_do_bestfit)) %>%
  mutate(
    coefficient = as.character(coefficient),
    coefficient = replace(
      coefficient, grepl("Intercept", coefficient), "b0"))

# Flowering probability
coef_fl <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_fl_bestfit)),
  value = coef(mod_fl_bestfit)) %>%
  mutate(
    coefficient = as.character(coefficient),
    coefficient = replace(
      coefficient, grepl("Intercept", coefficient), "b0"))

# Scape number conditional on flowering
coef_fln <- data.frame(
  coefficient = names(coef(mod_fl_n_bestfit)),
  value = coef(mod_fl_n_bestfit)) %>%
  mutate(
    coefficient = as.character(coefficient),
    coefficient = replace(
      coefficient, grepl("Intercept", coefficient), "b0"))

extr_value <- function(x, field) {
  subset(x, coefficient == field)$value
}
```

## Building IPM - Functions
```{r}
inv_logit <- function(x) {
  exp(x) / (1 + exp(x))
}


# Survival ---------------------------------------------------------------------
sx <- function(x, pars, num_pars = pars$mod_su_index) {
  val <- pars$surv_b0
  
  for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
    param <- paste0("surv_b", i)
    
    if (!is.null(pars[[param]])) {
      val <- val + pars[[param]] * x^i
    }
  }
  
  inv_logit(val)
}


# Growth -----------------------------------------------------------------------
grow_mu <- function(x, pars, num_pars = pars$mod_gr_index) {
  val <- pars$grow_b0
  
  for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
    param <- paste0("grow_b", i)
    
    if (!is.null(pars[[param]])) {
      val <- val + pars[[param]] * x^i
    }
  }
  
  val
}


# Growth variation -------------------------------------------------------------
grow_sd <- function(mu, pars) {
  sqrt(pars$a * exp(pars$b * mu))
}


# Growth transition ------------------------------------------------------------
gxy <- function(x, y, pars) {
  mu <- grow_mu(x, pars)
  
  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = mu,
    sd = grow_sd(mu, pars))
}


# Dormancy entry ---------------------------------------------------------------
dorm_x <- function(x, pars, num_pars = pars$mod_do_index) {
  val <- pars$dorm_b0
  
  for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
    param <- paste0("dorm_b", i)
    
    if (!is.null(pars[[param]])) {
      val <- val + pars[[param]] * x^i
    }
  }
  
  inv_logit(val)
}


# Flowering probability --------------------------------------------------------
fl_x <- function(x, pars, num_pars = pars$mod_fl_index) {
  val <- pars$fl_b0
  
  for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
    param <- paste0("fl_b", i)
    
    if (!is.null(pars[[param]])) {
      val <- val + pars[[param]] * x^i
    }
  }
  
  inv_logit(val)
}


# Scape number conditional on flowering ---------------------------------------
fl_n_x <- function(x, pars, num_pars = pars$mod_fl_n_index) {
  val <- pars$fln_b0
  
  for (i in seq_len(num_pars)) {
    param <- paste0("fln_b", i)
    
    if (!is.null(pars[[param]])) {
      val <- val + pars[[param]] * x^i
    }
  }
  
  exp(val)
}


# Recruitment size distribution ------------------------------------------------
re_y_dist <- function(y, pars) {
  norm <- pnorm(
    pars$U, mean = pars$recr_sz, sd = pars$recr_sd) -
    pnorm(
      pars$L, mean = pars$recr_sz, sd = pars$recr_sd)
  
  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = pars$recr_sz,
    sd = pars$recr_sd) / norm
}


# Reactivation size distribution -----------------------------------------------
react_y_dist <- function(y, pars) {
  norm <- pnorm(
    pars$U, mean = pars$react_sz, sd = pars$react_sd) -
    pnorm(
      pars$L, mean = pars$react_sz, sd = pars$react_sd)
  
  dnorm(
    y,
    mean = pars$react_sz,
    sd = pars$react_sd) / norm
}


# F-kernel ---------------------------------------------------------------------
fyx <- function(y, x, pars) {
  fl_x(x, pars) *
    fl_n_x(x, pars) *
    pars$fecu_b0 *
    re_y_dist(y, pars)
}
```

## Kernel
```{r}
kernel <- function(pars) {
  
  # Continuous active-size classes
  n <- pars$mat_siz
  L <- pars$L
  U <- pars$U
  h <- (U - L) / n
  
  b <- L + c(0:n) * h
  y <- 0.5 * (b[1:n] + b[2:(n + 1)])
  
  # Active survival and dormancy
  Smat <- sx(y, pars)
  Dmat <- dorm_x(y, pars)
  
  # Growth matrix
  Gmat <- matrix(0, n, n)
  Gmat[] <- t(outer(y, y, gxy, pars)) * h
  
  # Correct growth eviction
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    if (i <= n / 2) {
      Gmat[1, i] <- Gmat[1, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    } else {
      Gmat[n, i] <- Gmat[n, i] + 1 - sum(Gmat[, i])
    }
  }
  
  # Active -> active
  Tmat <- sweep(
    Gmat,
    2,
    Smat * (1 - Dmat),
    "*")
  
  # Active -> dormant
  Dorm_row <- matrix(
    Smat * Dmat,
    nrow = 1)
  
  # Dormant -> active
  React_vec <- react_y_dist(y, pars) * h
  React_vec <- React_vec / sum(React_vec)
  
  React_col <- matrix(
    pars$p_reactivate * React_vec,
    ncol = 1)
  
  # Dormant -> dormant
  Dorm_stasis <- 1 - pars$p_reactivate
  
  # Fertility from active individuals
  Fmat <- outer(
    y, y,
    Vectorize(function(y, x) {
      fyx(y, x, pars)
    })) * h
  
  # Full 201 x 201 kernel
  K <- rbind(
    cbind(Tmat + Fmat, React_col),
    cbind(Dorm_row, Dorm_stasis))
  
  return(list(
    k_yx = K,
    Fmat = Fmat,
    Tmat = Tmat,
    Gmat = Gmat,
    Dorm_row = Dorm_row,
    React_col = React_col,
    Smat = Smat,
    Dmat = Dmat,
    meshpts = y,
    h = h))
}
```

## Observed population growth
```{r}
# Count known living individuals. New adults are additionally counted one year
# earlier, matching the simplified recruitment assumption used in this IPM.

df_counts_alive <- df_ind %>%
  filter(state %in% c("active", "dormant", "alive_or_dormant")) %>%
  count(site, pop, qu, year, name = "n_alive")

df_newadult_backfill <- df_ind %>%
  filter(recruit_type == "new_adult") %>%
  transmute(site, pop, qu, year = year - 1) %>%
  count(site, pop, qu, year, name = "n_newadult_backfill")

# Use recruitment rows as the monitored quadrat-year inventory
df_counts_quad <- df %>%
  filter(row_type == "recruitment") %>%
  distinct(site, pop, qu, year) %>%
  left_join(
    df_counts_alive,
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  left_join(
    df_newadult_backfill,
    by = c("site", "pop", "qu", "year")) %>%
  mutate(
    n_alive = replace_na(n_alive, 0L),
    n_newadult_backfill = replace_na(n_newadult_backfill, 0L),
    n = n_alive + n_newadult_backfill) %>%
  group_by(site, pop, qu) %>%
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(
    year_t1 = lead(year),
    n_t1 = lead(n),
    annual_transition = year_t1 == year + 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(annual_transition)

# The final three transitions cannot fully resolve terminal dormancy
dormancy_cutoff <- 3
last_complete_transition <- max(df_ind$year, na.rm = TRUE) -
  dormancy_cutoff - 1

df_counts_year <- df_counts_quad %>%
  filter(year <= last_complete_transition) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_quads = n(),
    n_t0 = sum(n),
    n_t1 = sum(n_t1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(lambda_obs = n_t1 / n_t0)

df_counts_year

# Mean observed population growth
lam_obs_y <- df_counts_year$lambda_obs

lam_obs_mean <- mean(lam_obs_y, na.rm = TRUE)
lam_obs_geo <- exp(mean(log(lam_obs_y), na.rm = TRUE))

lam_obs_mean
lam_obs_geo
```
